title: Development of a Multi-Vendor DVR/NVR Forensic Analysis Tool for Standardized Acquisition, Recovery, and Analysis of Surveillance Evidence.
description:
• Background Digital/Network Video Recorders (DVR/NVRs) are widely used for surveillance in government agencies, law enforcement, critical infrastructure, businesses, and residential environments. Major DVR/NVR manufacturers such as Dahua Technology, CP Plus, Honeywell Security, TP-Link, Godrej, Uniview, HIKVISON, and Matrix use proprietary storage formats, file systems, metadata structures, and video encoding mechanisms. During forensic investigations, surveillance footage serves as crucial digital evidence; however, the lack of standardization across DVR/NVR vendors makes acquisition, recovery, analysis, and validation difficult. Investigators often rely on multiple vendor-specific tools, resulting in increased investigation time, inconsistent results, timestamp synchronization issues, challenges in deleted footage recovery, and difficulties in maintaining evidence integrity. Therefore, a unified vendor-agnostic DVR/NVR forensic analysis platform is required to provide standardized workflows for evidence acquisition, recovery, analysis, validation, and reporting.
• Description The proposed solution aims to overcome challenges such as non-standard forensic acquisition methods, proprietary file systems and video formats, difficulty in recovering deleted or damaged recordings, inconsistent timestamps, limited event correlation across cameras, challenges in maintaining chain of custody, dependence on multiple tools, lack of standardized reporting, and limited use of intelligent video analytics. The tool should support major DVR/NVR OEMs including Dahua Technology, CP Plus, Honeywell Security, HIKVISON, TP-Link, Godrej, Uniview, Matrix, and other commonly used platforms. It should automatically identify DVR models, parse proprietary file systems, create forensic images, extract videos and metadata, decode proprietary formats, recover deleted footage, normalize timestamps, generate cryptographic hashes (MD5 and SHA-256), correlate events across cameras, maintain chain-of-custody records, generate reports, and perform AI-based analytics such as face, object, and motion detection. Key modules include Device Identification, Acquisition, File System & Format Parsing, Recovery, Timeline Analysis, Reporting, and Machine Learning.
• Expected Solution The expected outcome is a software-based forensic platform capable of performing standardized acquisition, recovery, analysis, validation, and reporting of surveillance evidence across multiple DVR/NVR vendors. The solution should support at least five to six major DVR/NVR OEMs (Dahua Technology, CP Plus, Honeywell Security, TP-Link, Godrej, Uniview, HIKVISON and Matrix), provide a unified forensic workflow, reduce dependency on vendor-specific tools, automate evidence acquisition and analysis, improve deleted video recovery, ensure evidence integrity and admissibility, and generate comprehensive forensic reports. Deliverables include a comparative analysis of major DVR/NVR OEMs (Dahua Technology, CP Plus, Honeywell Security, TP-Link, Godrej, Uniview, and Matrix), DVR/NVR forensic Image, system architecture documentation, a functional prototype, Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), validation reports, user manuals, and a final project report. The tool should successfully parse proprietary file systems, decode video formats, recover deleted recordings,verify evidence integrity through cryptographic hashing, generate standardized reports, reduce analysis time, and produce reliable and legally defensible forensic results.
summary: Innovation (4/5): draws on ai, machine learning applied to a blockchain & cybersecurity problem, placing it in the breakthrough band. Feasibility (3/5): as a software build with moderate integration complexity, a full build is tight for 36 hours and will need scope-cutting. Impact (2/5): addresses a more targeted user group within Blockchain & Cybersecurity. Tech Depth (5/5): centers on architecture, infrastructure, standard. Sustainability (3/5): will need a maintenance/upkeep plan post-hackathon. Scalability (2/5): currently scoped narrowly and would need rework to scale. Total 19/30 -> Yellow verdict.

detail.title: Development of a Multi-Vendor DVR/NVR Forensic Analysis Tool for Standardized Acquisition, Recovery, and Analysis of Surveillance Evidence

overview.in_plain_terms: Build a forensic tool that can read and analyze surveillance video from many different DVR/NVR brands, each using their own proprietary storage format, giving investigators one standardized workflow instead of needing a different vendor-specific tool for each brand.
overview.why_it_matters: Surveillance footage is crucial evidence, but the lack of standardization across DVR/NVR vendors currently forces investigators to use multiple inconsistent tools, causing delays and integrity concerns in real cases.
pain_points: Major DVR/NVR vendors use proprietary storage formats, file systems, and encoding, with no standardization.
Investigators rely on multiple vendor-specific tools, increasing time and inconsistency.
Timestamp synchronization, deleted footage recovery, and evidence integrity are all genuinely hard across formats.
overview.background: DVR/NVR surveillance systems from many different vendors use proprietary, non-standardized formats, causing real investigative delays and inconsistency, a unified vendor-agnostic forensic tool is needed.
overview.whats_being_asked: A vendor-agnostic DVR/NVR forensic analysis platform providing standardized acquisition, recovery, analysis, validation, and reporting across multiple named proprietary vendor formats.
expected_solution: Standardized acquisition workflow across multiple DVR/NVR vendor formats.
Evidence integrity maintenance and standardized reporting.

analysis.innovation_scope_note: High. Genuine cross-vendor proprietary format reverse-engineering and standardization is real, hard forensic engineering, most existing tools handle only one or a few vendors.
analysis.invention_effort_note: High. Reverse-engineering proprietary storage formats for multiple named vendors (Dahua, HIKVISION, CP Plus, and others) without vendor documentation is genuinely difficult, specialized forensic engineering.

competitive_landscape.note: Highly specialized digital forensics niche, requires genuine reverse-engineering and file-system forensics expertise most teams won't have.

innovation.note: Genuine cross-vendor format standardization is real, valuable, and largely unsolved at this breadth in existing tooling.

invention.note: Reverse-engineering proprietary formats without vendor cooperation is genuinely difficult specialized work.

technical_feasibility.note: Full support across all named vendors in 36 hours is very ambitious; scoping to one or two vendors with genuinely reverse-engineered format support is realistic.

impact_and_benefits.note: Directly speeds up and standardizes real forensic investigations relying on surveillance evidence.

architecture.note: Format-specific parsers feeding a standardized analysis/reporting layer, real complexity concentrated in format reverse-engineering.

overall_verdict.reasoning: Strong pick for a team with real file-system/format reverse-engineering skill, scoped honestly to one or two vendor formats rather than claiming comprehensive vendor coverage.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: Very well-specified list of real vendor names and formats gives clear, concrete, checkable engineering targets.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: Claiming comprehensive multi-vendor support without genuine reverse-engineering work for each would be a significant overclaim, most real DVR forensic tools handle only a handful of vendors even as mature commercial products.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Scope to genuinely reverse-engineering and supporting one or two specific vendor formats (source sample footage/recordings from those vendors if possible) rather than claiming broad vendor-agnostic coverage you haven't actually built.

idea_0_4: Choose 1-2 specific DVR/NVR vendors to target, ideally ones with some existing public documentation or community reverse-engineering resources.
Source sample footage/recordings from your chosen vendor(s) if possible.
Split: one person on format reverse-engineering/parsing, one on the standardized analysis/reporting layer.
prototype_4_22: Reverse-engineer and build a parser for your chosen vendor's proprietary format.
Build deleted-footage recovery capability for that format if feasible.
Start the standardized analysis and timestamp-validation layer.
integration_22_30: Connect parsing, recovery, and analysis into one coherent workflow for your chosen vendor(s).
Test against real or realistic sample footage from your target vendor.
Build the standardized reporting output with evidence-integrity documentation.
polish_30_36: Polish the tool for genuine forensic-investigator usability.
Rehearse a live demo analyzing real or realistic footage from your chosen vendor format.
Prepare to be honest about your vendor-scope limitation versus the full multi-vendor vision.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Demonstrate your tool genuinely parsing and analyzing real (or realistically obtained) footage from your chosen vendor's actual proprietary format, that concrete, working format support for even one real vendor is more credible than a claimed broad multi-vendor capability.

strengths: Very well-specified vendor list gives clear, concrete targets.
Genuine, real investigative value if even one vendor format is properly supported.
weaknesses: Full multi-vendor coverage isn't achievable in 36 hours, requires honest scoping.
Proprietary format reverse-engineering without vendor cooperation is genuinely difficult, specialized work.

team_fit.ideal_ratio: Weight toward genuine reverse-engineering skill, that's the hard technical core of this PS.
team_fit.approach: Choose your target vendor(s) based on available sample data and any existing public documentation/community research to build on.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: The standardized analysis/reporting layer once format parsing is solved.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: The actual proprietary format reverse-engineering, that's genuinely difficult, specialized forensic engineering requiring real hands-on analysis of sample data, not something AI tooling solves generically.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: Claiming vendor format support without genuinely reverse-engineered, tested parsing would produce a tool that doesn't actually work on real footage from that vendor.

data_resource_availability.status: Real sample footage from specific DVR/NVR vendors may be obtainable (test devices, public forensic research samples); comprehensive samples across all named vendors are unlikely to be accessible.
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: Focus on 1-2 vendors where sample data or existing community reverse-engineering documentation is available.

judge_qna.question: How many vendor formats does your tool actually support, genuinely reverse-engineered and tested?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Be direct about your actual scope, 1-2 vendors with genuine, tested format support, rather than implying comprehensive coverage across all named vendors.
judge_qna.follow_up: What would be needed to add support for a third vendor format?

judge_qna.question: How do you maintain evidence integrity (chain of custody) throughout your acquisition and analysis process?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Describe your specific integrity-preservation approach, hashing, write-protection during acquisition, audit logging, this matters genuinely for real forensic admissibility.
judge_qna.follow_up: What happens if your recovery process encounters corrupted or partially overwritten data?
